This protocol applies to both research strands. It safeguards the privacy and confidentiality of participant data collected as part of the research study Troublesome Technologies and Learning Trajectories in Digital Preservation Practice. The definitions are aligned with the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR)1 and guidance from the Data Protection Commission (DPC).2

title: De-identification Protocol
section: Definitions
text:
Definitions







Term
Meaning




Personal data
Any information relating to an identified or identifiable natural person. Identifiers include names, identification numbers, location data, online identifiers, or factors specific to physical, genetic, mental, economic, cultural, or social identity.


Pseudonymisation
The processing of personal data in such a manner that the data can no longer be attributed to a specific data subject without the use of additional information. This additional information must be kept separately and subject to technical and organisational measures to prevent re-identification.


Anonymisation
An irreversible process that alters data so that the individual is no longer identifiable under any reasonable circumstances. While not explicitly defined in the GDPR text, anonymised data falls outside the scope of data protection legislation.

title: De-identification Protocol
section: De-identification procedures
text:
De-identification procedures
To adhere to data minimisation principles, the online survey collects no personal contact details other than an email address, which participants may voluntarily provide to take part in the follow-up research stage; names are collected only from participants invited to the interview stage. Each participant is assigned a sequential Participant Identification number (PID) based on survey completion. Key pairs linking PIDs to personal identifiers (such as name and email address) will be securely stored on a password-protected UCD cloud-based storage (Microsoft OneDrive) using multi-factor authentication, with access strictly governed by the principle of least privilege, restricting access exclusively to the PI and her collaborator. Data is stored in compliance with UCD IT security policies and hosted in secure European data centres (EEA) under UCD’s institutional data protection agreement with the service provider. The key pairs file will be permanently erased within 30 days of the conclusion of Strand 2 data collection.

title: De-identification Protocol
section: Protocol
text:
Protocol
This protocol ensures the protection of personal information and sensitive institutional details in research materials while maintaining enough context to allow a proper in-depth analysis. Upon explicit request, participants will be granted the option to review the de-identified written reflection and/or interview transcript to ensure their privacy is kept.







Element
Rule




Personal information
Participant names are replaced with standardised alphanumeric codes (e.g., PID020).


Colleagues and personnel
Non-participant individuals mentioned in text or transcripts are anonymised by omitting names and/or substituting functional roles (e.g., COLLECTIONS MANAGER), to preserve maximum fidelity to the source.


Institutions and organisations
Specific names of entities (e.g., libraries, museums, universities, companies, funding bodies, projects, or consortia) are omitted or replaced with broad category placeholders such as MUSEUM, UNIVERSITY, INDUSTRIAL PARTNER, SPONSOR, or PROJECT.


Locations
Specific cities or precise geographical indicators are omitted or replaced with placeholders like LOCATION, TOWN, MUNICIPALITY. Broader geographic contexts (such as countries) may be retained if they do not compromise anonymity.


Ellipses
Square brackets containing ellipses ([…]) signify where specific identifying details or context have been omitted to preserve confidentiality without disrupting narrative continuity.

title: De-identification Protocol
section: Application examples
text:
Application examples
The sample responses below, including all names, email addresses, specific organisational roles, project identifiers, and locations, are fictional examples artificially generated using Google Gemini 3.6 Flash solely for the purpose of demonstrating the enforcement of the protocol.

Online survey (open-ended questions)

Example A






Original



“When I was working as a Senior Archival Specialist at the Bodleian Libraries in Oxford between 2018 and 2021, I struggled heavily with setting up and configuring Archivematica (specifically version 1.7, which we had to run on an Ubuntu 16.04 server). My supervisor, Dr Marcus Vance, asked me to integrate it with our local DSpace repository…”








De-identified version



“When I was working as a Senior Archival Specialist at the UNIVERSITY LIBRARY (UK) […] between 2018 and 2021, I struggled heavily with setting up and configuring Archivematica (specifically version 1.7, which we had to run on an Ubuntu 16.04 server). My SUPERVISOR asked me to integrate it with our local DSpace repository…” In this instance, all references to specific locations and names have been omitted while preserving their participant’s role to ensure anonymity.




Example B






Original



“The primary difficulty stemmed from the complex XML configuration files for the METS/PREMIS metadata generation and rigid Micro-services architecture. Because our legacy digital collection—specifically the Evelyn Waugh Correspondence Collection (1930–1950)—had non-standard directory structures created back in 2012 by my predecessor, Julian Ross, the automated ingest pipelines kept failing at the normalization step.”








De-identified version



“The primary difficulty stemmed from the complex XML configuration files for the METS/PREMIS metadata generation and rigid Micro-services architecture. Because our legacy digital collection—specifically the SPECIAL COLLECTION […]—had non-standard directory structures created back in 2012 by my PREDECESSOR, the automated ingest pipelines kept failing at the normalization step.”





Written Reflections

Example A






Original



“I heard you’re taking over the automated web archiving transformations for the Bristol City Council contract. Since I spent most of October 2023 pulling my hair out over Preservica Enterprise Cloud, I wanted to write down a few things I wish someone had told me on day one. When Heritage Data Solutions won the Council contract under David Miller’s oversight, I was expecting Preservica to have a modern, drag-and-drop workflow builder. Instead, I discovered that customising ingest pipelines for large-scale WARC files required building complex, nested XML logic manually through their API endpoints.”








De-identified version



“I heard you’re taking over the automated web archiving transformations for the CITY COUNCIL (United Kingdom) contract. Since I spent most of October 2023 pulling my hair out over Preservica Enterprise Cloud, I wanted to write down a few things I wish someone had told me on day one. When INDUSTRIAL PARTNER won the Council contract under PROJECT LEAD’s oversight, I was expecting Preservica to have a modern, drag-and-drop workflow builder. Instead, I discovered that customising ingest pipelines for large-scale WARC files required building complex, nested XML logic manually through their API endpoints.”




Example B






Original



“I heard you’re taking over the digital forensics workflow for the Dr Arthur Pendelton collection. As I spent most of late 2021 battling BitCurator on that exact project, I wanted to pass along a few survival tips before you dive into the deep end. When I first took on the collection at the Smithsonian in August 2019, I naively thought running digital forensics would be as simple as inserting media and clicking “extract.” But once Michael Chang in IT set up my Linux virtual machine with BitCurator 2.0, reality set in fast.”








De-identified version



“I heard you’re taking over the digital forensics workflow for the SPECIAL COLLECTION […]. As I spent most of late 2021 battling BitCurator on that exact project, I wanted to pass along a few survival tips before you dive into the deep end. When I first took on the collection at the MUSEUM (United States) in August 2019, I naively thought running digital forensics would be as simple as inserting media and clicking ‘extract.’ But once IT STAFF set up my Linux virtual machine ([…]) with BitCurator 2.0, reality set in fast.”





Interview Transcripts

Example A






Original



“Marcus Thorne: For me, the prior experiences that helped were less about software and more about systems troubleshooting and high-pressure project management. Before I joined Heritage Data Solutions in Bristol, I spent three years as a Digital Records Officer at the Bath & North East Somerset Council, working under a project director named Jonathan Hayes. Back in 2020…”








De-identified version



“PID020: For me, the prior experiences that helped were less about software and more about systems troubleshooting and high-pressure project management. Before I joined INDUSTRIAL PARTNER in LOCATION (United Kingdom), I spent three years as a Digital Records Officer at the LOCAL COUNCIL (United Kingdom), working under a PROJECT DIRECTOR […]. Back in 2020…”




Example B






Original



“Eleanor Vance: The second key experience was an introductory Python and Bash command-line module I had taken during my MA at UCL in 2017, taught by Prof. Alan Greenwood. At the time, I passed the module and immediately went back to traditional archival theory, thinking I’d never need to look at a terminal again. However, when my supervisor, Dr Marcus Vance, asked me to resolve those METS/PREMIS normalisation failures, I wasn’t starting entirely from zero. Because of Prof. Greenwood’s class, terminal commands didn’t look like complete gibberish to me…”








De-identified version



“PID115: The second key experience was an introductory Python and Bash command-line module I had taken during my MA at UNIVERSITY (United Kingdom) in 2017, taught by PROFESSOR. At the time, I passed the module and immediately went back to traditional archival theory, thinking I’d never need to look at a terminal again. However, when my SUPERVISOR asked me to resolve those METS/PREMIS normalisation failures, I wasn’t starting entirely from zero. Because of PROFESSOR’s class, terminal commands didn’t look like complete gibberish to me…”

In particular, it seeks to understand what makes particular digital technologies troublesome to learn, how practitioners respond to these difficulties, what strategies and workarounds they develop, and which sources of knowledge and support they draw upon as they build competence.

section: Introductory statement - invitation to take part
text:
Introductory statement - invitation to take part
Thank you for your interest in the second phase of our research study, ‘Troublesome Technologies and Learning Trajectories in Digital Preservation Practice’. When completing the Strand 1 survey, you indicated that you would be open to participating in a follow-up activity.
We now invite you to participate in Strand 2, which consists of a written prompt-guided reflection and, for selected participants, a short online interview, each estimated to take 15-20 minutes. In this strand, we aim to delve deeper into the specific technology learning hurdles you identified in the survey, exploring the professional contexts, informal coping strategies, and support systems you used to navigate them.
Taking part in this research is entirely voluntary. Please review the complete details of the Participant Information Leaflet below before deciding whether to participate.

title: Participant Information Leaflet (S2)
section: What is this research about? Why is this study being done?
text:
What is this research about? Why is this study being done?
Digital preservation involves the practices and technologies used to ensure that digital materials remain accessible and usable over time, despite technological change, media failure, organisational change, and other challenges. This research explores how digital preservation practitioners experience and navigate these learning challenges throughout their professional trajectories. In particular, the study seeks to understand what makes particular digital technologies troublesome to learn, how practitioners respond to these difficulties, what strategies and workarounds they develop, and which sources of knowledge and support they draw upon as they build competence.
This second strand builds directly upon the online survey, using qualitative methods to capture richer, nuanced narratives about real-world learning trajectories in digital preservation practice.

title: Participant Information Leaflet (S2)
section: Why have I been invited to take part?
text:
Why have I been invited to take part?
You have been invited because you completed the Strand 1 online survey, voluntarily provided your email address to express interest in the follow-up study, and met the inclusion criteria for the research (self-identifying digital preservation practitioner aged 18 or over, with at least one year of professional, practical experience in digital preservation or a closely related area, experience of working with digital technologies, and hands-on experience in an organisational setting).

title: Participant Information Leaflet (S2)
section: Do I have to take part?
text:
Do I have to take part?
No. Taking part is entirely voluntary. You do not have to give a reason if you choose not to take part, and there will be no negative consequences for you if you decide not to participate.

title: Participant Information Leaflet (S2)
section: What will happen if I decide to take part in this research study? What do I need to do?
text:
What will happen if I decide to take part in this research study? What do I need to do?
Strand 2 involves two components:

Written Reflection: You will receive an email invitation containing your personalised reflection prompt (reflecting the technology you identified in Strand 1) and a personal link to an online form hosted on SurveyMonkey. The form presents the informed consent declaration and the option to type your reflection into a text box or upload it as a file (approx. 15-20 minutes to complete, though writing paces may differ among individuals).
Short Semi-structured Interview: Depending on participant selection for this final step, you may also be invited to participate in a short online follow-up interview (approx. 15-20 minutes) conducted via UCD’s institutional Zoom platform to discuss your experience and anything that emerged from your written reflection in greater detail.

We encourage participation in both activities if you are selected and available; however, partial completion (taking part in the written reflection only) is fully respected. Indicating interest or completing the written reflection does not guarantee an interview invitation, nor does it oblige you to take part if invited. If you participate in an interview, it will be audio-recorded using UCD’s institutional Zoom account for accurate transcription. You may keep your camera turned off if you prefer, as only the audio is required for our analysis.

title: Participant Information Leaflet (S2)
section: Can I withdraw from the study? What happens if I change my mind?
text:
Can I withdraw from the study? What happens if I change my mind?
You may withdraw from Strand 2 at any time, without giving a reason, by contacting the research team. Because Strand 2 data is pseudonymised during collection, any written reflections, audio recordings, or interview transcripts you provide can be completely deleted upon request at any time prior to the end of February 2027 (30 days following the conclusion of Strand 2 data collection). At that point, key-linking files are permanently destroyed, rendering the dataset fully anonymous, and individual responses can no longer be identified or removed. If you withdraw from Strand 2, please tell us whether you would also like your Strand 1 survey answers removed. Withdrawing will have no negative effect on you.

title: Participant Information Leaflet (S2)
section: What are the benefits of my participation in this research: to me, to the researchers, and to any third parties involved?
text:
What are the benefits of my participation in this research: to me, to the researchers, and to any third parties involved?
Taking part in this study may not directly benefit you, although many participants find that reflecting on their career trajectories and learning experiences is a valuable professional exercise. Your detailed accounts will help us better understand how practitioners build competence as technologies, standards, and systems change.
The outcomes of this study could benefit the wider digital preservation community, as well as educators and professional bodies that design training and professional development. The research also supports the academic work of the researchers, including scholarly publications and presentations. Interview transcripts will be generated using UCD’s institutional Zoom account and checked by the research team; no third-party service provider gains any benefit from your data, and under UCD’s enterprise agreements your data will not be used to train commercial AI models.

title: Participant Information Leaflet (S2)
section: What are the risks of taking part in this research study?
text:
What are the risks of taking part in this research study?
There are no anticipated major risks. Some participants may experience mild discomfort when recalling challenging or stressful learning experiences; you retain full control over what details you share. Because digital preservation is a relatively small professional field, there is a minor risk that someone could recognise you from specific details in a narrative answer (such as a unique job title or specific workplace setting). To mitigate this, the research team will screen and de-identify all written text and interview transcripts prior to analysis and publication (on request, you may review the de-identified version of your written reflection and/or interview transcript), following our project’s De-identification Protocol.

title: Participant Information Leaflet (S2)
section: How will I find out what happens with this research study?
text:
How will I find out what happens with this research study?
The findings from this research study will be reported in academic publications and presented at conferences, workshops, teaching, and other research or professional events. If you would like to receive information about the outcomes of the research, you can contact the research team using the contact details provided below. No information revealing your identity will ever be disclosed in any report or publication.

title: Participant Information Leaflet (S2)
section: Data protection
text:
Data protection

What information about me will be used in this research study?
We will use your email address (and, if you are invited to an interview, the name you give us when booking) strictly for research management purposes; your written reflection responses, and—if invited to participate in the short interview—the audio recording and transcript of that conversation will be used in qualitative data analysis. We do not intend to collect special-category personal data (such as information about your health, political opinions, or religious beliefs) as part of this study. Please avoid including such information in your responses. Technical telemetry data, such as IP addresses and location details, are disabled on the SurveyMonkey platform by the research team to ensure response privacy.


How will my data be used?
All written reflections, audio recordings, and transcripts will be stored in UCD’s OneDrive, protected by multi-factor authentication. Written reflections submitted via SurveyMonkey will be transferred to OneDrive and deleted from SurveyMonkey once data collection is complete. For interviews, only the audio recording and its transcript will be transferred from Zoom to OneDrive; the copies held on UCD’s Zoom account are then deleted manually by the research team. If the quality of a Zoom transcript is insufficient, the de-identified transcript may be corrected using Google Gemini or, as a fallback, Microsoft Copilot Chat, in both cases through UCD’s institutional account. Under UCD’s enterprise agreement, these data are not used to train AI models or reviewed by humans. UCD records prompts and responses for security and compliance purposes, subject to its access controls, and the research team will delete the chat history after each use. All transcripts are checked and corrected by the research team against the audio. Derivative datasets will be exported for qualitative analysis (using CAQDAS software such as NVivo or Atlas.ti), de-identified prior to analysis. Analysis files will be stored in UCD OneDrive and accessed strictly on multi-factor authenticated devices by the primary research team. Using your unique Participant ID (PID), we will cross-reference your Strand 2 responses with your Strand 1 survey submission to contextualise your narrative. Anonymised quotations and qualitative themes may be included in academic publications and other research outputs.
After publication, the anonymised dataset may be made available to other researchers for future research related to the aims of this project, in line with UCD research data management requirements. Your contact details, original audio recordings, and key-linking files will never be shared with anyone except the research team.


Who will have access to my personal data? What will happen to my personal data?
UCD is the data controller primarily responsible for protecting your personal data. Only the primary research team (Assoc. Prof. Amber Cushing and Dr Giulia Osti) will have access to identifiable data, key-linking files, and raw recordings. SurveyMonkey (used for the online form), institutional cloud platforms (Microsoft 365 Enterprise), Google Gemini and Microsoft Copilot Chat (used only where needed to correct de-identified transcripts), and Zoom process data on UCD’s behalf under formal enterprise agreements with UCD and may not use it for their own purposes, including training AI models.


How will my personal data be protected? Will it be kept confidential?
Your identity will be kept strictly confidential. You will keep the same Participant ID (PID) that was assigned to you in Strand 1. Key pairs linking PIDs to personal identifiers (such as your name and email address) will be kept in password-protected, encrypted UCD-approved cloud storage (OneDrive) accessed with multi-factor authentication, accessible strictly by the PI and Dr Osti.
Your email address and name will be kept separate from the dataset used for analysis and will never appear in the research dataset, publications, or other outputs. All research data are stored in UCD’s OneDrive and on SurveyMonkey’s EU-based servers, and any de-identified transcripts corrected with AI tools are processed within UCD’s EU-based institutional environments; all are located within the European Economic Area (EEA), in compliance with UCD IT security policies.


How long will my data be retained by this project?
The key linking your Participant ID (PID) to your personal contact details will be permanently deleted within 30 days after the conclusion of Strand 2 data collection, by the end of February 2027. Standalone email contact lists will be erased at the same time. Audio recordings stored in OneDrive will be permanently deleted as soon as transcripts have been verified and de-identified; the copies held on Zoom are deleted manually by the research team as soon as they have been transferred to OneDrive. The de-identified research dataset and analysis derivatives, which contain no personal or sensitive data, will be retained for 10 years following publication or public release of the work, in line with the UCD Research Data Management Policy.


What is the lawful basis to use my personal data?
UCD relies on the legal bases of Article 6.1(a) (Consent) and Article 6.1(e) (‘Public Interest’ / Public Task) of the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) to process your personal data. Should any special category (sensitive) personal data be provided accidentally in text or spoken responses, Article 9.2(j) (‘Scientific Research Purposes’) applies, and the data will be redacted immediately. Giving consent for data processing under GDPR is separate from ethical consent to take part in the research.


What are my rights?
You are entitled to:

Withdraw your consent at any time;
Object to UCD’s use of your personal data or any further use;
Request access to your personal data and to receive a copy of it (up to the point of full anonymisation, when key-linking files are destroyed);
Request inaccurate personal data be corrected or deleted;
Request restriction of UCD’s use of your personal data (if it is inaccurate); and
Request deletion of your data, if no longer needed.

By law, you can exercise the above rights in relation to your personal data unless certain limitations apply, for example where the request would make it impossible or very difficult to conduct the research or put the quality of the research findings at risk (such as after data have been fully anonymised or published).


Contact details
If you have questions or require reasonable accommodations/adjustments to complete the survey, please contact the research team. If any questions are not answered in a satisfactory manner, contact can be made with the UCD Data Protection Officer. Finally, if none of the UCD contacts have given a satisfactory response, you have the right to lodge a complaint with the Data Protection Commission.

Assoc. Prof. Amber Cushing: amber.cushing@ucd.ie

UCD Data Protection Officer (DPO): gdpr@ucd.ie
Data Protection Commission (DPC): https://forms.dataprotection.ie/contact

What will happen if I decide to take part in this research study? What do I need to do?
You will complete an online survey that takes about 9-12 minutes. It runs on SurveyMonkey, and you can complete it on any web browser and device. The survey asks about your professional background, current role, work environment, career experience, learning pathways, and experiences with digital technologies that you have found challenging to learn. Some questions ask you to reflect on difficult learning experiences, and some ask for short written answers.
You choose which experience to discuss and how much detail to give. You do not need to disclose anything you consider sensitive, confidential, or identifying, and if you encounter questions you prefer not to answer, you can withdraw at any time before submitting the survey by closing your browser window.

Once submitted, fully anonymous responses cannot be identified or removed. However, if you voluntarily provide your email address to express interest in the follow-up study, your survey answers become pseudonymised. In this case, you may request the removal of your survey answers and/or withdraw your expression of interest at any time before the end of February 2027 (when the linking key is destroyed) by contacting the research team. Withdrawing will have no negative effect on you.

What information about me will be used in this research study?

Your survey responses will be analysed using statistical analysis and qualitative thematic analysis to examine troublesome technology experiences in digital preservation practice. De-identified quotations and aggregated statistics may be included in academic publications and other research outputs. We will take steps to remove identifying information from material used in research outputs.
We do not intend to collect special-category personal data (such as information about your health, political opinions, or religious beliefs) as part of this study. Please avoid including such information in your responses. Technical telemetry data, such as IP addresses and location details, are disabled on the survey platform by the research team to ensure response privacy.


How will my data be used?
The information collected through this survey will be used for the purposes of this research project and to inform participant selection for the qualitative follow-up stage. Findings from the survey will be reported in academic publications, conference presentations, teaching materials, and scholarly outputs.
Raw responses collected via SurveyMonkey will be exported to and stored in the institutional cloud-based storage service (Microsoft OneDrive), protected by multi-factor authentication. Once data collection is complete, all responses will be permanently deleted from the SurveyMonkey platform. Preprocessing and initial data management will occur within UCD’s Microsoft Enterprise environment, and any derivative datasets exported for statistical analysis (using software such as R or Python) will be de-identified or anonymised by default prior to analysis. Analysis files will be stored in UCD OneDrive and accessed strictly on multi-factor authenticated devices of the research team.
After publication of the research findings, the anonymised dataset may be made available to other researchers for future research related to the aims of this project, in line with UCD research data management requirements. Your email address and the link to your survey responses will never be archived or shared.


Who will have access to my personal data? What will happen to my personal data?
UCD is the data controller primarily responsible for protecting your personal data. Only the primary research team (Assoc. Prof. Amber Cushing  (Principal Investigator) and Dr Giulia Osti  (Co-investigator / Research Enquiries)) will have access to survey responses and email contact details.
SurveyMonkey processes survey data on its EU-based servers under a formal enterprise agreement with UCD and may not use it for its own purposes. The project funder does not receive any personal or identifiable participant data. Written responses will be screened and de-identified by the research team according to the project’s De-identification Protocol before data are analysed, archived, or used in outputs.


How will my personal data be protected? Will it be kept confidential?
The survey is anonymous unless you choose to give your email address. If you do not give your email address, we collect no information that identifies you. If you give your email address, it is collected in the last section of the survey and separated from your answers when the data are exported, so that it is stored apart from your survey answers.
A Participant ID (PID), assigned arbitrarily by the research team, links your email address to your survey responses. We need this link so that, if you are invited to the follow-up study, the invitation can refer to your survey answers. Until the key link is deleted, your survey responses are pseudonymised (linked to an ID, not to your name) rather than fully anonymous. The list linking PIDs to email addresses is kept in password-protected, encrypted UCD-approved cloud storage (OneDrive) accessed with multi-factor authentication, and only the Principal Investigator and Dr Osti can access it. Your email address will be kept separate from the dataset used for analysis and will not appear in the research dataset, publications, or other outputs.


How long will my data be retained by this project?
The key linking your Participant ID (PID) to your email address will be permanently deleted by the end of February 2027. The de-identified survey dataset and analysis derivatives, which contain no personal or sensitive data, will be retained for 10 years following publication or public release of the work, in line with the UCD Research Data Management Policy. Email addresses and any other personal data are not retained beyond the deletion date above.


What is the lawful basis to use my personal data?
UCD relies on the legal bases of Article 6.1(a) (Consent) and Article 6.1(e) (‘Public Interest’ / Public Task) of the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) to process your personal data. Should any special category (sensitive) personal data be provided accidentally in open text fields, Article 9.2(j) (‘Scientific Research Purposes’) applies, and the data will be redacted immediately. Giving consent for data processing under GDPR is separate from ethical consent to take part in the research.


What are my rights?
You are entitled to:

Withdraw your consent at any time;
Object to UCD’s use of your personal data or any further use;
Request access to your personal data and to receive a copy of it (up to the point of anonymisation);
Request inaccurate personal data be corrected or deleted;
Request restriction of UCD’s use of your personal data (if it is inaccurate); and
Request deletion of your data, if no longer needed.

By law, you can exercise the above rights in relation to your personal data unless certain limitations apply, for example where the request would make it impossible or very difficult to conduct the research or put the quality of the research findings at risk (such as after data have been fully anonymised or published).
